platforms.title: 3 Signs Your Cold Has Turned Into Sinusitis
platforms.meta_description: A cold that improves and then suddenly gets worse again isn't always just a lingering cold. How to recognize bacterial sinusitis and know when to see a doctor.
platforms.body_html:
Ever felt like a cold was finally clearing up, only to have it suddenly hit hard again a few days later? The American Academy of Otolaryngology flags that "better, then worse again" pattern as a classic sign of bacterial sinusitis. It's different from an ordinary cold just dragging on, and it can call for its own kind of care.

Why a cold can turn into sinusitis

A cold is a viral infection that inflames and swells the nasal lining, and most of the time it clears up on its own within 7 to 10 days as the immune system fights off the virus. But sometimes that swelling blocks the small openings that drain the sinuses — the air-filled spaces next to the nose. Mucus gets trapped inside, and bacteria can multiply in that trapped mucus, turning into a secondary bacterial sinusitis.

According to the American Academy of Otolaryngology, the biggest risk factors are nasal allergies, a deviated septum, smoking, a recent cold, and swimming or diving. Water pushed into the sinuses during swimming can carry bacteria along with it, which is part of why these factors make bacterial sinusitis more likely.

How to tell it apart from an ordinary cold, and when to see a doctor

First, symptoms lasting more than 7 to 10 days without any real improvement. An ordinary cold usually shows at least some gradual improvement over time; the absence of that trend is worth noticing.

Second, feeling better for a few days and then suddenly having the fever return and pain worsen. That "double worsening" pattern is the most distinctive sign to watch for. Facial pain or pressure that gets worse when bending forward makes it more likely still.

Discharge color alone isn't a reliable way to tell — yellow or green mucus shows up in ordinary colds too. What actually matters is the duration, the double-worsening pattern, and facial pain together. Swelling around the eyes, vision changes, or severe headache with confusion are rare but genuine emergencies that need care right away.

Even when it is bacterial, most sinusitis improves with supportive care like saline nasal rinses and staying well hydrated. If the pattern above is clear and persists, a doctor may consider antibiotics, but a simple viral cold doesn't need them.

That distinction matters beyond just this one illness. Taking antibiotics for a cold that's purely viral doesn't speed up recovery at all, and it also contributes to antibiotic resistance over time, making infections harder to treat down the road for everyone. Keeping rough notes on when symptoms started, whether there was a stretch of feeling better before things turned worse again, and how the facial pain behaves when bending forward gives a doctor much more to work with than trying to summarize a vague, days-long history from memory during a short appointment.

The takeaway: a cold that improves and then suddenly worsens again, or drags on past 10 days, is worth having an ENT check for bacterial sinusitis. This article is for general health information; consult a medical professional for diagnosis and treatment.
